subsubtopic: REQUESTED COMMITTEE STUDY OF INTEREST RATE POLICY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
On Wednesday, October 10, 1979, the House unanimously accepted a motion which reflected the understanding of members of all parties of the impact of high interest rates and inflation on Canadians in all walks of life. The prime rates then were 15 per cent and inflation was 9 per cent. Today prime rates are 17 per cent and inflation is 12 per cent.
1 therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), the exact same motion proposed on October 10, 1979, by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Chretien), and consistent with remarks made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in the House yesterday, February 17, 1982:
That this House immediately order its Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs to be set up and that the committee undertake an immediate review of the interest rate policy of this government and of the Bank of Canada, and that for this purpose the governor of the bank and the Minister of Finance appear before it to explain their actions and what they will be doing to solve the problems the governor of the bank himself said interest rates are now causing for individuals and to business.

speechtext: Thank you, Madam Speaker. It is a little difficult to be heard over the hubbub. I want to address a question to the minister responsible for housing. I ask the minister how does anyone explain that to people who cannot find affordable housing, who have to go into housing which costs far more than they can reasonably be expected to pay?

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-93, to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join in this continuing second reading debate on Bill C-93, which is one of those common but regrettably deceptive bills the government has a habit of bringing in. It has a very innocent title- "An act to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes and to provide other authority for the raising of funds." It is an apples and oranges bill consisting of a borrowing authority, which is the apples part, taxes in the form of a natural gas and gas liquids tax and a petroleum gas revenue tax, which is the oranges part. This bill arises out of a budget brought down in October, 1980, almost a year and a half ago.
The borrowing authority provision, we argue should more properly be considered as a separate piece of legislation since it deals with a totally different subject from petroleum taxes. However, we are stuck with the fact that these two mixed items, and I believe inappropriately mixed, are considered in one bill. Therefore, we are forced to debate what amounts to two different subjects on the same occasion and vote on what amounts to quite separate principles. So be it. My colleagues have debated at some length the implications of the borrowing authority. Therefore, I would like to concentrate my remarks primarily on the oranges part of this bill, the petroleum and gas revenue tax and the natural gas and gas liquids tax.
These two taxes arose out of the National Energy Program, which was part of the 1980 budget brought down October 22, at which time these provisions were introduced. Given that fullness of time, it is interesting to look back at the National Energy Program to see what was promised and compare it to what was delivered to see what new nirvana the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), promised us when they introduced the budget in 1980. It is interesting to see what hell has, in fact, ensued as a consequence of this budget and the accompanying national energy policy.
The national energy policy had three goals-security of supply, Canadianization and fairness of revenue sharing. These were magnificent goals, goals that no Canadian could oppose in terms of their objectives. But what has happened? What has this program led to? What is the reality as opposed to those statements of intent?
February 18, 1982

First let us look at the question of self-sufficiency. The minister of energy informed this Flouse that there would be no question but that Canada would be energy self-sufficient by 1990 because of the extraordinarily good energy policies that he and his colleagues had brought in. What is the reality? There is not a single, knowledgeable individual or organization in this country that believes that assertion by the minister. There is not one, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, the National Energy Board, an independent body, after having held months of extensive public hearings across the country, and with the best information available to it, in its report in June, 1981, after looking at various alternatives, reported at page 9:
The board is not forecasting oil self-sufficiency in either of the above cases.
In other words, in terms of any of the alternatives the board looked at and any assumptions it could make, the board could not see oil self-sufficiency. In this connection the board was looking at the year 2000. The National Energy Board says that Canada will not be self-sufficient by the year 2000 based on the government's energy policies. Does that stop the minister of energy? Not at all. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources issues a press release saying that Canada will be self-sufficient. Why will Canada be self-sufficient? Because the minister of energy says so. Is there any evidence to that effect? There is not. The minister of energy says that Canada will be self-sufficient because a combination of the Alsands and Cold Lake projects, together with a conservation program, will make it possible. There are also some heavy upgrade programs that will help in this objective.
Let us look at what has happened. The Cold Lake project is dead. The Alsands project looks like it is dead. It is taking a while to die, but it certainly looks as though it will die. The heavy oil upgrading program of Polysar, which was a big part of the program the minister was trumpeting about in October, is dead. These things which the minister was counting on are dead. But what did the minister say last week when these facts were brought to his attention by a reporter with a good filing system? The minister said, "Well, we do not really need Alsands and Cold Lake anyway; we will be self-sufficient as a result of east coast offshore and Beaufort." II we take a look at what the minister said a year ago, we find that he said, "We are not counting on Beaufort or east coast offshore to make us self-sufficient. We are not counting on that; we will be self-sufficient because of Alsands, Cold Lake and these heavy upgrading programs."
If you were to buy a used car from the minister, Mr. Speaker, you would deserve to buy a lemon. The fact is, that because of the incredible incompetence of this government, self-sufficiency is out the window. We had better all pray that some new equivalent of the Ayatollah Khomeini does not come along. We had better pray that that madman in Syria, Assad, can keep those madder men in the city of Hama, who are trying to impose a Khomeini-type revolution in that country, under control. If anything happens in any Middle East country or in any other of the single-party states around the world upon which we rely for oil, then we will find ourselves in a pretty pickle indeed. But not to worry; by then the minister of
Taxation
energy and his colleagues will be long gone and will not be held accountable or responsible for the situation. We know that they will have no consciences to bother them about the legacy they have left to Canadians of the future.
What about the second part of the program, that of Canadi-anization? We are going to Canadianize the oil and gas industry. 1 heard the minister say that. He.said that he was going to Canadianize the oil and gas industry by having at least 50 per cent of the industry owned by Canadians by the year 1990.
The minister did not tell the House how he would achieve that. It was not by having the Canadian part grow but by having the foreign part shrink. What we will be doing is making sure the oil and gas industry is such a smaller component than it used to be; the Canadian component of 50 per cent will be 50 per cent, but 50 per cent of a whole lot less than it was. The hypocrisy of the minister is absolutely mind-boggling.
One wonders about the editorial writers at the Ottawa Citizen who rate this minister as an A-l minister. You wonder if they can read, if they keep records. Do they remember what in fact has been said? As just one example, Mr. Speaker, in July, 1981, the Canadian Development Corporation bought out the shares of Elf Aquitaine, a 75 per cent French-owned company. According to The Globe and Mail, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said, in talking about the agreement between the CDC and Elf Aquitaine:
-the agreement was very welcome and demonstrated that the federal government's policy of increasing Canadian ownership of the oil industry is being carried out "expeditiously and effectively".
That is what the minister said; Canadianization is working. Well, Mr. Speaker, on January 30, 1982, the minister was in France, the country that used to own 75 per cent of Elf Aquitaine. Speaking of the France-Canada Chamber of Commerce, it is reported that:
He also made a strong appeal for increased French investment in Canada, particularly in the energy sector, in a speech at a luncheon meeting of the France-Canada Chamber of Commerce.
In July, 1981, he said "Hallelujah, Canadianization is working because we bought out this French-owned company." In January, 1982, he is in France saying. "We would like French money to come over here and invest in the oil and gas industry." He is trying to suck and blow at the same time. But that does not prevent George Radwanski of the Toronto Star saying what a great minister this is, that he is Canadianizing. On this same trip he stopped in Paris en route from Kuwait where he was trying to encourage the Kuwaitis and others in the Middle East to invest in Canadian energy projects. First he announces to great acclaim, fanfare and the singing of "Hallelujah, we are going to Canadianize, buy out these rotten foreigners;" and then announces with great pride and wide smiles, "1 have talked the Arabs and French into investing in Canadian energy projects." If you bought a used car from that man, Mr. Speaker, you deserve to have a lemon.

February 18, 1982
Taxation
The reality is, Mr. Speaker, that the National Energy Program had nothing to do with self-sufficiency or Canadiani-zation. It was simply gimmicky phrases utilized, effectively I admit, by the government. What that policy was really all about was indicated by the minister in a speech in Sherbrooke, Quebec, on October 22, 1981, when according to the Canadian Press he said:
-a stronger threat to Canadian unity than Quebec nationalism could soon be posed by the growing wealth of Alberta. The other nine provinces would eventually be at the mercy of Alberta's every fancy, he said, and a wave of Alberta nationalism of unprecedented strength could rise up if the federal government held back now from showing its teeth. "We don't pay enough attention to this threat.'' I.alonde said, "but it's a real one. it's there."
Well, Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the Alberta provincial riding of Olds-Didsbury we had the result of this minister baring his teeth. For the first time outside the province of Quebec Canadians voted for a separatist because of the policies of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who says that a bigger threat to Canadian unity than Quebec nationalism is Alberta's wealth. And to that kind of behaviour the Ottawa Citizen says A-l. I hope and pray, Mr. Speaker, that the message the people of Olds-Didsbury were trying to send yesterday will be heeded by some responsible people opposite. Hopefully there are some in that Liberal Party somewhere who will heed that message, who will say to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and others who feel they can strengthen national unity by beating on the heads of western Canadians: Stop! We want this whole country to stay together. We do not want Canadians to feel that their national government does not represent them. We do not want Canadians to turn in frustration to separatism because they cannot get the attention of their supposed national government.
This feeling, Mr. Speaker, which exists in Olds-Didsbury and elsewhere, indeed I might say the feeling which exists in knowledgeable people here in central Canada-and there are some-is a reflection of the NEP and what it is doing. Because the fact of the matter is that that program, particularly as exemplified by the taxes in this bill, the petroleum and gas revenue tax and the natural gas and gas liquids tax, is hurting Canadian companies more than it is hurting the foreign multinationals which supposedly are the villains and the ones we are supposed to be hitting.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that the NEP hit Canadian-owned companies harder than foreign-owned companies. That is not my opinion, that is not information from a suspect source; that is from the Petroleum Monitoring Agency of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the minister's own department. This report, which came out about six weeks ago, covers the first six months of 1981; in other words, the first six months of full operation under the NEP. It shows that the result of the NEP is that during that time foreign-owned companies suffered a 28.5 per cent income drop in their Canadian operations. In comparison, Canadian-owned companies suffered a revenue drop of 52 per cent. So, Mr. Speaker, for the purposes of Canadianizing the industry we
introduce taxes which hit Canadian-owned companies twice as hard as foreign-owned companies.
The NEP, Mr. Speaker, has in fact driven Canadian companies out of Canada. The Petroleum Monitoring Agency report shows that Canadian-controlled junior companies increased their foreign exploration in the first six months of 1981 by 247 per cent as compared with the first six months of 1980. They were driven out of Canada. There was a 247 per cent increase in foreign operations by Canadian companies which were driven out of Canada by a government which says it will Canadianize the oil industry. That was a blatant falsehood, an out and out deception.
The reality is that the minister spoke the truth in Sherbrooke when he said that the object was to put those westerners in their place, to bare their teeth, because wealth in Alberta cannot be tolerated and is a threat to national unity. How effective were they? Again, the Petroleum Monitoring Agency, which obtained its data from StatsCan, showed that during the first six months of 1981 the petroleum industry earned an average return on capital employed of 9.4 per cent. It is something 1 will want to deal with very extensively before we complete all stages. 1 refer to the provision "whereas the rate of tax can be set by regulation".
If that is permissible, the next logical step is that the Income Tax Act will say tax rates will be set by regulation, the Excise Tax Act will say that the tax rates will be set by regulation and in fact the Crown will assume to itself the right to set all taxes. The historical rationale behind Parliaments, the reason for the Magna Carta, that the Crown shall not tax without the approval of Parliament, shall have been violated. This is a precedent that should terrify anybody but the most doctrinaire socialist who believes the government should do whatever it wants, whenever it wants, because the government knows all and has all wisdom, intelligence and so on.
This will be a matter that I and my colleagues will want to pursue with some vigour. This House would be committing a tragedy and leaving a legacy for the nation, in terms of this procedent if we allow it to pass, where the Crown by regulation can set tax levels. The power to tax is the power to destroy. To put the power to destroy in the hands of the Crown without a parliamentary check-and there would be none under this precedent-is so extreme that it is almost incomprehensible that something like that would be contemplated.

was based on the supposition, admitted reasonably based at the time, that world energy prices would increase at inflation plus 2 per cent.

I can assure the House that people in the rest of the country are suffering as well, albeit second-hand, but many of the unemployed in central Canada are unemployed as a result of that consequence.

I hope more than just a few of us examine this precedent of taxation by order in council. If we allow that to happen, 1 am afraid one of the most fundamental freedoms in a democracy, freedom from arbitrary taxation levels by the Crown, will have been destroyed. If we are to fulfil our responsibilities as representatives of the people, we must not let that happen.

He was pro-Crow, but the hon. member on my right was anti-Crow. Was he pro-Joe or anti-Joe? I suppose he is not telling. It is rather sad to see the party tearing itself apart when there is so much room for ammunition to throw across the floor.
Another myth is that somehow the boom was ended in western Canada by a coalition of Liberal and NDP ideas. 1 remind the House that the NDP is not in power in British Columbia, Alberta or Ottawa. A likeminded government is in power in Saskatchewan, and its economy is relatively healthy.
The final myth is the entire Conservative position. What is its position with respect to energy? It is that we should let foreign capital come in and make Canada a big Bermuda. Surely there is a fundamental flaw in the position. If the hon. member listened to his own words, he would see the flaw. The fact is that foreign capital will come in and, when investors do not like it here or find greener pastures elsewhere, they will go to Denver or Indonesia.

speechtext: Do you want a banana republic?

That could be. I listened to the comments of the Conservative energy critic and one of his distinguished colleagues who is a member of the energy committee. Its strategy seems to be to solely let foreign capital come in. It is willing to repeat past mistakes and continue that way, but I do not think it will hold up.
I should like to make some reference to the separatist victory in the provincial byelection in Alberta yesterday. As a western Member of Parliament, I should like to make a couple of comments about it. Basically I see it as a collapse of the Social Credit Party in Alberta and as an indication of disappointment and disillusionment with the Lougheed government. It is an attack on the Lougheed government as well as on government in Ottawa. Ottawa has not been listening to the problems of the people of that area. As I deal with the budget provisions in my speech, I hope to show where improvements could be made to those policies. I wish people in eastern Canada would really try to understand some of the problems of western Canada. I understand the difficulty of understanding when one hears idle rhetoric such as the allegations of the last two speakers. If westerners could be faulted at all, I suppose we could be faulted for not articulating our position clearly. The position certainly exists, and the east is not listening.
There are perhaps three traditions in western Canada which are never reflected in the eastern press or in the words of
eastern members of the House. There is a sort of wild, anti-Ottawa, populist tradition which fluctuates up and down; perhaps it is somewhat redneck. It was reflected in the byelection.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Would the hon. member clarify what he means by eastern press? Was he referring to the press of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, or was he talking about the press of Ontario and Quebec?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am from Vancouver and any press east of Cranbrook is eastern press, such as The Calgary Sun and so on. Perhaps I will give the hon. member an example. Recently an article appeared in the Toronto Star, a very good newspaper, which referred to this nonsense about all the power in Canada suddenly moving to Calgary and that Calgary would surpass Toronto in the near future; it was absolute nonsense. I am glad to see Calgary and the province of Alberta growing, but in the near future it will not surpass the power and influence of Toronto. In my view that is stupid journalism.
I should like to return to what I was saying about traditions in western Canada. The first tradition is that rather odd populist tradition about which I talk. It is reflected in this separatist victory, and I think it is an aberration which will go away. It is not similar to the situation in Quebec which I think is a more fundamental problem.
The second tradition is the Conservative tradition, the legitimate Conservative and private enterprise tradition of the west. This tradition has been reflected in many speeches, sometimes with less rhetoric, by hon. members on my right. Those speeches are worth listening to, although I disagree with them in terms of the Conservative position. It is a legitimate tradition, but it is not the only tradition of the west.
The third tradition is that of socialism and co-operation. It has existed in western Canada for some time and it is a growing tradition. It is reflected in the governments of Manitoba and Saskatchewan and in the opposition of British Columbia. It has a different focus; perhaps it is a little more people-oriented in a different sort of way. It believes that government is not the big bad wolf. It believes in government initiative and direction. It believes in co-operative federalism between federal and provincial governments. It is somewhat populist and anti-Ottawa. It is looking at decentralization and participation in government in different ways. It is looking at reform of existing political structures. I am a member of that tradition because I like to think it is the way of the future. There is a sense of outrage in the west, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) indicated.
There has been a housing crisis in Vancouver for three years. Just last week there were reports in Ottawa that vacancy rates were low and that housing prices were rising; I bet we will now see some government action on housing. Although we yelled and screamed about the housing crisis in British Columbia, the whole crisis was ignored by Ottawa.
February 18, 1982

We have seen government members rise and dismiss our objections regarding the Crow rate as reactionary. It is easy for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to do that. It sounds good and the whole eastern press-this time east of the Lakehead-picks it up and indicates that it is reactionary. But they have not examined the real situation. Westerners feel that is part of the bargain of confederation. If you change the grain rates, you have to change a lot of other things as well; for instance, some of the bargains that westerners made with the national policy of eastern Canada, the tariffs, the anti-Crow position, and so on. This should not be dismissed so easily.
I want to say something about the National Energy Program. This program is a limited success. It is perhaps the only success of this government. The direction of the program is correct. I said that in this House in June, 1980, before the program was introduced. The public want more. The committee to Canadianize released a poll showing that the public supported public ownership of the oil industry. I think the public is in favour of greater Canadianization. You have to distinguish the vocal critics from the majority of the people of this country. The hon. member from Calgary reflects the oil industry. Of course, Imperial is not very happy about this program. It does not want to give up any of its profits. The crucial point is that oil is a strategic commodity. That is where the National Energy Program and the Conservative Party differ.
This is not putting westerners in their places. The oil is there in the west. The same problem will arise with Newfoundland and with the north when development starts up. Oil is a strategic commodity and has to be developed through public direction. You cannot have a few cowboys being totally free to run the industry. That does not stop private initiative in the industry, but you have to have some overriding direction.
There are problems with the National Energy Program which are not helped by this bill. The program has not attracted small Canadian industry to the frontier. It has attracted big corporations and foreign-owned corporations. The government will have to take another look at that.

The second problem is the slow rate of Canadianization. We now have an industry which is 60 per cent to 65 per cent foreign controlled. The government has said it is not going any further with Canadianization. The government has stopped the procedure. That is the problem with the Liberals; philosophically, they cannot complete a progressive program. I hope some day there will be a realignment in this country between a conservative group and a progressive group.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
There is; it is the Progressive Conservative Party.
Taxation

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Not a Progressive Conservative group. But 1 think the realignment will come about.
The third problem with the National Energy Program, and 1 think the hon. member from Saskatchewan who preceded me is right about this, is that the little guys are not being helped. There seems to be evidence that drillers and small companies are not being helped. Perhaps that is the reason the Conservatives did not do very well in the byelection. Premier Lougheed has not protected small drillers, neither has the National Energy Program. The government of Saskatchewan took some steps with respect to royalties. That government is rebating and reducing royalties to help small drillers. That sort of thing should be looked at. I hope members opposite will not call me a doctrinaire free-enterpriser for saying that.
In my opinion, it is a false premise that the National Energy Program will take us to self-sufficiency. Right now we import 20 per cent of our oil. The established remaining reserves of conventional oil in western Canada amount to about five billion barrels. We have about ten years of reserves at the present rate of consumption. The Hibernia reserves are projected to come on stream in 1986, which will bring in an additional 1.5 billion barrels of oil. But there will be delays with this project. Hon. members are aware of what happened the other day and the tragedy that ensued on the oil rig there.
The Beaufort Sea has a potential of about ten billion barrels of oil, but that oil will be hard to extract. We have not yet recovered a drop from there. That Arctic islands, especially the Cisco find offshore Lougheed Island, is very promising. There is a potential five billion barrels in the north. However, we have no way of getting that oil to market. The tar sands projects are delayed. There are technical problems today with both Suncor and Syncrude. The Alsands project is not finance-able. That is why the companies are coming to the federal government for welfare. They want both the federal government and the government of Alberta to bail them out and subsidize the program. That is not at all promising. Cold Lake is a better project. Maybe we can get 450,000 barrels from the tar sands by the early 1990s. Drilling for gas has declined in western Canada whereas drilling for oil has increased.
Let us try to deal with the facts, not rhetoric. It seems to me the problem with the National Energy Program is that it concentrates on the supply side. Instead, we should be looking at the demand side and putting some money into the area of conservation and alternate energy. When we reach the energy security legislation I propose to go into greater detail about how we can conserve and move to alternate energy instead of spending $4 billion in PIP grants.
Specifically, I want now to give some of our positions on Bill C-93. First, it deals with offshore. That point has to be addressed. It is a very difficult problem. Hon. members might note that the Ottawa Citizen took me to task in an editorial. It can be found in "Quorum". The Citizen took Premier Peel -ford and me to task for trying to "exploit" the Hibernia crisis because we complained about overlappingjurisdictions. I think it was a pretty shameful editorial. In fact, I think it was a low blow.

February 18, 1982
Taxation

1 do, and 1 suspect the hon. member over there agrees with me. He has a right to ask questions about Hibernia and about safety. He has asked questions and so have his colleagues. 1 have a right to ask questions too.
There are nine conflicting jurisdictions in the federal government. Two inquiries are under way, and with the Americans joining in there will be a third. Both the federal government and the Newfoundland government are trying to shirk responsibility for the accident. What about the American government? Who has jurisdiction? I think that is a legitimate point to raise. I think the editorial in the Ottawa Citizen is pretty disgusting. The editorial is also inconsistent.
When Bill C-48 was being debated, editorials and news reports in the Ottawa Citizen said that we should be looking into all these matters of oil spills, safety and so on. But when we start asking questions about them, the Ottawa Citizen criticizes us. Journalists have every right to criticize us; politicians are fair game. But in this case I think the criticism is wrong and the writers have been inconsistent. I have a perfect right to say that.
Basically, the provinces should have jurisdiction over offshore, but we should have interlocking jurisdiction. Under Section 91 of the British North America Act, the federal government has jurisdiction over navigation, ports, defence, external affairs and fisheries. Unless we amend the Constitution they will remain, no matter which way we decide about the offshore.
1 do not agree that we should spend three years on this matter by going to the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and then working up through the Court of Appeal. Let us go now if the governments cannot decide. I would prefer a negotiated settlement, but if the governments cannot decide the matter should be referred immediately to the Supreme Court of Canada. The disaster in Hibernia shows that we have to solve some of these problems. And if the Ottawa Citizen wants to criticize me for this, it can do so.
As a westerner 1 know how control of our resources has fueled our growth. I think that is something that should be considered soon. Meanwhile 1 think the minister was right to include in the bill the clause on the offshore because if they are subsequently changed by virtue of agreement with the provinces or by virtue of the Supreme Court decision, it is important that we have them there.
With respect to Clauses 4 and 5, Mr. Speaker, the tax on domestically consumed natural gas, we are happy that the government for once listened to western Canada and did not put a tax on export gas. Western Canadians said, how come they are going to put a tax on the export of our gas and not on electricity from Quebec or Ontario? It was hard to explain that, so the government quite properly, after questions in this House, withdrew that proposal and then proposed a tax on domestically consumed gas.
The problem with that, and I say this to the minister, is that it is a regressive tax. Hon. members recall the Liberals promised in the 1980 election that we would have lower energy prices. In fact, they gave us higher energy prices. They argue that they had to raise prices, but if you do that you should redistribute some of the extra money. If you are going to tax low-income people, the old and the poor, as you do with this tax, you should give them some of it back in the form of a cost of living tax credit. I think that makes sense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: We did give it back, lan.

I do not think it has been given back. Total energy costs, as measured by a component of the CPI, have gone up 46 per cent since 1980 under the Liberals. Natural gas prices went up 28 per cent in 1981. The present cost to consumers for oil and gas will double by 1986. I hear from my riding about increased hydro and gas bills, and I suspect other members from British Columbia are hearing it. It is regressive and is hurting older people and those on fixed incomes.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the petroleum and gas revenue tax, the PGRT, is a very complicated matter but 1 will try to make it as simple as I can. Simply put, it is a royalty. It has a certain advantage because you put it on at the wellhead and you cannot deduct this tax here or this expense there. The Conservative government was going to put the tax on at the refinery, the infamous 18-cent-a-gallon tax which some commentators said was responsible for our being here today in these particular positions. The problem with the tax is that it seems to be hurting some of the small producers. As I said previously, it may be the obligation of the federal or provincial governments, following Saskatchewan's lead, to alleviate that problem somewhat. Rather than just export our gas, I suggested a gas bank, because we may need it since we have been converting to gas in eastern Canada. In any case, 1 will have detailed questions on that when we deal with the bill.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have alleged, and it has never been denied, that there has been a windfall gain for the oil companies for one quarter of 1981 in which no higher taxes were levied. What happened was that the government boosted the price by $2.50 a gallon for the three months from October 1 to December 31, 1981, but the taxes did not come in until January 1. So a government which says they talk tough to the oil companies to turn around and give them a windfall creates a bit of a credibility gap. I hope to explore that when we go into the details of the bill. 1 see the minister nodding, and 1 will put those questions to him or the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
I would like to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying something about the myth of the megaprojects. This great spin-off of jobs, and so on, is a myth. There are a lot more jobs in all kinds of other projects. I was counsel to the Mackenzie Valley pipeline inquiry and used to hear these great stories about all the jobs that a megaproject like a pipeline would create. However, when you got into it and examined the witnesses, you found there were a few construction jobs for basically foreign welders who travel around the
February 18, 1982

world doing that. There were some jobs for small construction companies, and there were a few security jobs after it was built. And you were paying $10 billion to build it.
So we have to have a debate in this House, I hope soon, on what I call the myth of the megaprojects. I know the government likes these projects. 1 suspect Canadians have bought the myth that we have to get these megaprojects going to produce jobs, but 1 think it has to be looked at very carefully. The hour for that debate is coming because we are going to look at the Alsands project in some detail.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to warn the government that they are running the risk, in the agreement with Alberta, that the Canadian price of oil may be more than the world price by 1985. There is a glut on the market, world prices are falling, and there is a clause in the agreement that our price be no more than 75 per cent of the world price for old oil, and no more than 100 per cent for new oil. However, that does not include all the special taxes and levies, so it is possible-and this would be most ironic for a Liberal government elected two years ago today partly on a promise of lower energy prices, certainly less than world prices-that they may have put us in a position where we will go beyond world prices. If that happens then there will have to be a renegotiation of the agreement with the producing provinces.
Having given that dire warning, and having dealt, 1 think, with the many aspects of this bill relating to energy, I will sit down and let the government ponder those allegations.
