That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all correspondence, memoranda, records of telephone conversations and other communications between the Department of National Health and Welfare and the appropriate ministers of the governments of the provinces relating to the standards for programs and the conditions for federal participation in a revised Canada Assistance Plan.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in this federal government structure there are many sacred cows. Certainly the Canada Assistance Plan is one of those sacred cows. Any suggestion concerning the existing legislation or its administration which might be considered critical is immediately implied to be a criticism of the objectives of the plan itself.
I hope to allay any fears that I am in any way criticizing the objectives of the Canada Assistance Plan. However, the Canada Assistance Plan is financed by the federal government on roughly the basis of 50 per cent of the costs incurred by the provinces. I say "roughly", because the federal government itself imposes the terms and conditions under which it will make the payments. The provincial governments render an invoice, in effect, to the federal government, and the federal government pays according to the amount of invoice submitted. This year, the amount estimated to be paid by the federal government was some $2 billion. However, just last week in the House, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) told us that the amount which was to be paid this year had increased by some 19 per cent, 19 per cent being approximately $400 million. Therefore, the payments this year from the federal treasury will be of the order of $2.4 billion. If one multiplies that by two and then adds some more, the "some more" being the additional amounts paid by the provinces, one can see that we are looking at an expenditure in the social service field considerably in excess of $5 billion.

February 18, 1982
Canada Assistance Plan
It is interesting to note that during this year, the Quebec province share of the $2.4 billion which is being paid out of the federal treasury is of the order of $700 million, or, per capita, between $160 and $170. One can compare that with the other provinces. The next highest province is the province of Newfoundland, at $96. One notes that the per capita payment in Ontario is $77. These figures, incidentally, were produced by the department for the benefit of a committee which was looking into the Canada Assistance Plan earlier in 1981.
For the record, I would like to look at the two parts of the program. I will divide it into what I shall term as the social assistance programs, which are payments to persons with no other source of income, such as the disabled, single parents with children, those whose unemployment insurance payments have run out, and so on. The federal government has a very direct interest in these particular social assistance programs because it has a tremendous influence on the need at that level. It does have that influence because of federal programs such as the old age pension at one end of the age scale, and the family allowances program at the other end of the age scale.
I referred earlier in my remarks to sacred cows, and I want to interject at this point to say that one of the sacred cows is the subject of universality. That irritates me somewhat. There seems to be all-party support for universality, but there is certainly nothing universal about the programs as they are presently applied, for example, to the old age pension. The major benefit of the old age pension program goes to those who receive the supplement which, of course, is income tested. In the case of the child tax credit, it goes to those with the greatest need, whereas family allowances, of course, are paid to everyone right across the board.
The point I am making is that universality is an excellent objective and one which I would strongly support; but from all practical points of view, we cannot infer that our programs are universal, for the reasons I have stated. I have often made two suggestions. One may not be popular with all my constituents, but I do not mind as 1 have made this public. I suggest that we should stop increasing old age pensions and increase the supplement by an additional amount. Thus, if we were to index, we would index only on the supplement plus the old age pension and, of course, we would have some additional funds so that we would be able to increase the amount of the supplement.
At the other end of the scale, I have suggested that we completely eliminate the family allowances scheme and that we fold the total amount of this program into the child tax credit. While I am referring to the child tax credit, one of the urgent things we must do is to substantially reduce the limit up to which a child tax credit is paid.
1 shall put on the record what may be a somewhat amusing story, but in a certain sense, I think, it is also critical. I was astonished last year to receive from my accountant, who looks after my individual tax returns, a document under which my wife was able to sign her name and apply for a relatively small refund, but, nevertheless, a refund from the federal government under the child tax credit plan. Of course, Your Honour
is aware that I have two children. However, I found it rather ridiculous that I was in the position of receiving a child tax credit. Furthermore, the amount was not very much because 1 was obviously right at the top of the scale. I do not need to disclose what the salary scale is for Members of Parliament because it is public knowledge. However, because 1 was at the top of the scale, the child tax credit was quite small. One could imagine my feelings, almost amounting to anger, or my intrigue when from my accountant I received a bill for preparing that return amounting to some $40, which was more than four times the amount of the child tax credit!
Just to complete this little story, the bill which I received from my accountant for the preparation of my tax return was deductible. Therefore, I put it in, and because I paid taxes at approximately 50 per cent, 50 cents on the dollar, I therefore saved $20 out of the federal treasury. Therefore, the federal treasury paid $20, I paid $20, and my wife received $10. That was a pretty good deal, and 1 have put this story on the record because I think it is time that we looked at the administration of these programs. I think I have made it clear here that 1 am not criticizing the program itself.
The other part of the Canada Assistance Plan on which I wanted to spend some time is the social service area. This includes the personal services or welfare services, including day care, homemakers, counselling services, child welfare, etc. I have suggested that we should get out of social services and do so by transferring the tax room to the provinces.
Never!
I heard the word "never" from the NDP.
What happened to health care when you did that?

First of all, this is the position of the Quebec provincial government. They believe that since they administer these programs, they should have full control over them, finance the programs themselves and should not have to go cap-in-hand to the federal government. If you look at these programs in detail, you find that there is a tremendous variation from province to province. The federal government simply says, "Send us the bill and we will pay 50 per cent".
I have already mentioned the amount per capita in Quebec. The split in that province for social assistance programs, is approximately $94 per capita this year. Those are the programs in which the federal government has a tremendous influence, as I have already explained. The payments for social service programs or welfare services over which the federal government exercises no influence whatsoever approximate to $44 per capita in the province of Quebec.
Many of the programs shared under CAP are delivered by non-governmental organizations such as Children's Aid Societies, which are given enforcement responsibility for functions such as the apprehension of children. In some provinces,
February 18, 1982

particularly Ontario, municipalities play a significant role in the delivery of both social assistance and social services.
Many groups maintain that they have insufficient information about what is cost shareable under the CAP. For example, the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled had argued that voluntary organizations and disabled individuals need to be better informed of the potential benefits available through CAP so they can lobby their provincial governments effectively. Municipalities in Ontario, charged with the delivery of general welfare assistance and many social services, complain that they do not know whether the rules governing their funding are provincial or federal.
Municipalities may not even be privy to the contents of the federal-provincial agreements. This is the subject for discussion this afternoon. As a result, they do not know whether the rules regarding services are needed to conform with Canada Assistance Plan requirements or are simply rules established by the provincial government.
Health and Welfare Canada occasionally issues guidelines on what is cost-shareable in terms of dollars and specific criteria. It is these guidelines that present problems of understanding the limits of CAP for the public and social agencies. These guidelines have not generally been made public.
The special committee to examine federal-provincial fiscal transfer payments recommended that, and 1 quote:
-the Minister of National Health and Welfare have a Canada Assistance Plan manual compiled to include all guidelines, notes and administrative directives, and that this manual be made public, with appropriate provision to respond to questions by the public on its application.
Objections at the provincial government level are based on the totally unacceptable assumption that the release of these documents would facilitate their municipalities in making interprovincial comparisons. It should be noted that even under the proposed freedom of information act, items which could be detrimental to federal-provincial relations can be exempted from release.
1 had put a notice of motion for the production of documents on the Order Paper. In November of last year I received a copy of the latest signed agreement between the government and the province of Ontario under the Canada Assistance Plan. It is a very voluminous document. I would suggest that no one rush to get a copy. First, it includes the memorandum of agreement made on March 28, 1967. pursuant to part 1 of the Canada Assistance Plan. Attached to that document is a listing of amendments. For example, I will refer to the last three in the pile. There is one made October 31, 1979, listed as Amendment No. 34. Amendment No. 35 is dated September 15, 1980, and Amendment No. 36, the last one in the pile that I was given, is dated February 20, 1981.
All these documents provide is a listing taking off certain locations, certain institutions that are no longer to be financed under the Canada Assistance Plan, and adding on other institutions and listings. This is interesting reading. 1 have no idea whether it is an issue in the respective provinces, but if any provincial social welfare groups have need of this document, I
Canada Assistance Plan
will be very pleased to supply them with a copy. Of course, it is now in the public domain.
I should also advise them that the documents in the other provinces under Motions Nos. 74 to 82, which are the corresponding agreements in the nine provinces, other than the province of Ontario, have been delivered to me. They are in my possession and are available to anyone interested in seeing them. Unfortunately, they do not include the real information, the regulations. These are in the hands of the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I would like to read three short extracts from a letter from the Department of National Health and Welfare for the benefit of members of the special committee on federal-provincial fiscal transfer payments to which I referred earlier. I quote:
-shareable welfare services under the plan are being provided in all provinces, to a greater or lesser degree.-
Provincial definitions of "social services" may not necessarily be consistent with CAP's definition of "welfare services".-
Provinces may provide services which arc recognized welfare services for cost-sharing purposes under CAP, e.g., daycare, but if CAP requirements arc not met, sharing is only partially available or not available at all.
The important sentence reads as follows:
-the provinces arc not required to submit detailed information on individual services-
Enough is enough. Whether the members of this House agree with my attitude toward the division of social services and social assistance programs is irrelevant. 1 accept and recognize that there is unlikely to be any major change in this regard. 1 put my opinion on the record for what it is worth. However, I believe that the information on the type of programs that are being funded, the extent to which they are being funded, and the criteria under which they are being funded should be available for all members of the public in order that they can compare. The provinces may be somewhat afraid because they realize that this could lead to additional claims. It could lead to pressure from the public to provide in one province the kind of service that is provided in another province.
The reason I have brought this motion forward is that I believe the information should be on top of the table. Whatever we as individuals may desire to do in changing the administration or the legislation, the fact that the program exists means, in my opinion, that the public should have full access to all the information which will enable the public to make maximum use of the program while it is in force and in the fashion in which it is in force.
1 have brought this matter forward for debate simply because I recognize that what I am asking for, which is the discussions which are presently under way, is not likely to be provided before the expiry of the period at which time a new agreement has to be signed. It is just as well to allow interested members to express their opinion on what they would like to see in the revised Canada Assistance Plan which will become operative at the start of the next fiscal year.

February 18, 1982
Canada Assistance Plan

Mr. Speaker, the motion brought before the House by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) raises two questions of real concern and interest to all members of the House. First, there is the matter of the free flow of information and the need for freedom of information legislation which would allow Members of Parliament, and all Canadians, to have access to any information from the government necessary to make a study, form an opinion or evaluate a government program. I am always willing, as I am sure are many other members, to support the need and desire for freedom of information legislation to allow this information to flow without the need of special or formal steps to be taken within the procedures of Parliament.
As you may know, Mr. Speaker, there is a piece of freedom of information legislation before the House in the form of an access to information and privacy act. However, that bill has been delayed in committee and the minister in charge has indicated that he may withdraw the bill. This is, indeed, unfortunate, because without the freedom of information legislation, which would require the government to produce information which ought to be made available for the study and assessment of government programs, we will have to continue to use these parliamentary devices to obtain that information. There is a general solution available to the problem of government information being unobtainable. That is the channel we should follow in order to obtain information. We cannot do this until legislation is presented and enacted by the House.
The second matter which the motion brings forward is the status of the Canada Assistance Plan. I would like to make some general remarks about the Canada Assistance Plan and the social services program which is based on that legislation.
I worked for some years in provincial government administration and 1 remember the state of social services legislation which existed in provinces like Nova Scotia, even as late as the early 1950s. At that time, there was a mass of provincial legislation dealing with such programs as mothers' allowance under which support was provided for unwed mothers, mothers who were separated or widowed and those who had no other means of support. There was also the blind persons' allowance and a myriad of provincial legislation which provided necessary welfare benefits.
I know the same was similar in other provinces. During the 1950s, the provincial and federal governments attempted to bring some order to this morass of provincial and federal welfare legislation. What eventually emerged was the Canada Assistance Plan which became a statute of the Parliament of Canada. There was similar legislation under various names in most provinces.
The purpose of this legislation was to codify in a very clear and formal way the base for social services. The Canada Assistance Plan, which was enacted in 1966 or 1967, became the base for our modern and current social service system. Unfortunately, 15 years later that social service system is in jeopardy as a result of the financial policies which were
brought forward by the Canadian government in the budget of November, 1981.
1 would like briefly to illustrate the effect of the budgetary provisions which were introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). As I have said in the House and elsewhere, the minister has proposed to transfer the federal deficit to the provinces. The result will be that those provinces which are now in a deficit position will simply not have sufficient funds to contribute to those social service programs, educational services and health services. They will not have the financial ability to maintain these services.
I would like to pay particular attention to that fact because it is supported by the Economic Council of Canada. The Economic Council has said that this is the thrust of the budget provisions with respect to the reduction of the federal deficit. The Economic Council of Canada has confirmed that this will flow through to the provinces in the form of cutbacks on the available funds for health, educational and social services. We must be wary of this and bring it to the attention of Canadians.
I would like briefly to talk about those services which are available and will be until March 31, 1982 under the Canada Assistance Plan and supporting provincial legislation. There are a wide variety of services available and I would like to indicate the effect of those services. According to my statistics, which relate to 1978 and 1979-the numbers are probably much higher for the current fiscal year-approximately $1.6 billion was spent under the Canada Assistance Plan. There were 1,547,000 Canadians who received benefits in all the provinces and territories of Canada under programs which were included within the Canada Assistance Plan. These programs constitute a broad range of social service programs under the Canada Assistance Plan. We should not forget that the Canada Assistance Plan and its services are in addition to programs such as old age security and many other programs which are funded through the provinces and the federal government.
The programs we are talking about in relation to the Canada Assistance Plan deal primarily with assistance to persons in need. These programs include welfare services for those needy persons or those likely to become in need, as well as work activity projects.
If we look at what is occurring in our cities, towns, villages and rural areas, we will see people who, for various reasons, cannot provide for their own welfare. In some cases, they may have reached the age where they can no longer work to support themselves, there may be people who are mentally or physically disabled, or there may be cases where there are children whose parents are not able to provide for them. I am sure that all Canadians recognize that there are many people who find themselves in these unfortunate circumstances in our society.
1 believe that the role of the Canada Assistance Plan is clearly established. I cannot believe that any Canadian-
February 18, 1982

certainly not any Member of Parliament-would be in favour of abolishing any of the programs which have been proven to be essential and necessary. There should be no question of abolishing or cutting back these programs, but rather how these programs can be rendered more effective and efficient. If there are to be any savings or cutbacks on the use of public funds, they should be used to make these programs more effective and efficient.
It is easy to speak with conviction on these matters when you are from the maritimes and a province like Nova Scotia. The services, which are included in the Canada Assistance Plan and supporting provincial legislation, are absolutely essential although a great drain on the revenues of the government. 1 have statistics which demonstrate this fact clearly. In Newfoundland, for example, 17.9 per cent of all provincial expenditures are for social service programs. In the province of Nova Scotia, 20 per cent of all government expenditures are on social services. For the province of New Brunswick, the figure is 19 per cent. These provinces also spend a great deal of their available revenue on education and health. In Newfoundland, approximately 46 per cent of total government revenue is spent on education and health. In Nova Scotia, it is 42 per cent.
It does not take a great deal of imagination to realize that the Atlantic provinces spend a vast amount of their available revenue on programs which are related to education, health and social services. At the same time those provinces have to incur deficits which ultimately have to be supported by taxes. If these deficits are increased it is not hard to see that those provinces will be financially unable to continue those services at the level which was enjoyed in the past.
We are at a point in our history when we ought to be improving those services and ensuring all Canadians have a decent way of life and a decent lifestyle. As I have said, we know there are many Canadians who simply cannot do it on their own and need help.
When we talk about social services and programs and the financial ability of provinces to provide those programs to their people so there will be equality across Canada, it is interesting to note how the provinces spend their money. For example, it will surprise no one that the province of Alberta is number one on the list of per capita expenditures. The government of the province of Alberta spends $3,135 per person on government services. It is also interesting to note that the poor little province of Prince Edward Island is next on the list. The province of Prince Edward Island spends $2,618 per person to provide services to the individuals of that province.
Statistics such as these demonstrate graphically that the province of Alberta, with its great wealth and resources, is able to spend $3,135 per person for government services, and it is easy to see how that province can afford that kind of money, but we must ask ourselves how the province of Prince Edward Island, which is next on the list, at $2,618, can afford to maintain those services. Bearing in mind that this province has
Canada Assistance Plan
a budgetary deficit and bearing in mind that it has a permanent government debt, I can tell hon. members that if there is any cutback in transfer payments to that province, it will not be able to maintain the services, and that if this province has the desire to maintain services, it will only do so through increased taxation. This is a very serious situation, and it is not helped-it is rendered more extreme-by the budgetary provisions. The message we as members of the House of Commons have to get out to Canadians is how budgetary provisions and government financial policies affect the services Canadians require.
Let me talk very briefly about the system in use under the Canada Assistance Plan. As I have said, it covers a variety of services which are directed to persons in need, and those persons quite often are senior citizens, disabled persons and the young. The method by which those services are delivered is through provincial social services departments and the municipalities, which maintain departments to provide social services. In most cases there are financial tests which are the bases for administering those services. In some cases the financial tests are quite difficult; that is to say, people who may feel they need government assistance are not able to get it because they do not qualify under the financial test.
This raises a matter which was discussed earlier and referred to as the matter of universality in government programs. It is true that in bringing in old age assistance and many other assistance programs, the federal government established the principle-if we can call it a principle-of universality; that is to say, if there is assistance available to persons of a certain age-in the case of old age assistance the age is 65 and over-it ought to be given to all persons who reach that age and ought to be universally applied and should not be based on any kind of need or means test. Even though universality is a matter of principle which commands broad support, there comes a time in our history when we cannot afford that kind of program; that is to say, our desire to provide assistance to a group of persons without reference to their special financial needs affects our ability to provide effective services to those who really require the services. As has been pointed out, I think it is true that we must review the principle-if we can call it a principle-of universality. We must make sure people are not being deprived of necessary and essential services merely because we are trying to conform to a principle which can no longer be practically applied.
I agree that we ought to examine universality and consider tests and methods which will identify those in our society across Canada who need service at public expense. We ought not to waste our financial capability by providing services to persons who do not really need them.
In my view-and I am sure in the view of most members of the House-there is no way the federal government ought to get out of the field of providing social services. That would be a tremendous danger, not just to the individuals who might be affected but to the whole fabric of Canadian society. In addition, it would contradict the very idea of the constitutional changes which have finally been approved in the House. It

February 18, 1982
Canada Assistance Plan
would contradict the idea that Canadians right across the country ought to have equal services. The new constitutional provisions indeed indicate that the government ought to direct its attention toward the removal of any causes of regional disparity. It ought to take action which will allow people in the maritime area to enjoy the same level of service and standards as those enjoyed by persons in central Canada and western Canada. If the federal government at this stage of our development were to vacate the field of social services, that would be a disaster. The federal government has that obligation, the obligation has been accepted and this is no time to reject it.
I am afraid there is some truth to the suggestion that the federal government is getting out of social services because I have indicated-and I do not want to repeat it-that it has been demonstrated by this budget that the federal government is in fact reducing its assistance to the provinces in the way of transfer payments and in the way of support for established programs. This indeed could lead to withdrawal of social services and services which are now being provided in the educational and health fields. Again we must be on guard to ensure that the federal government does not go too far down this road because that would have a disastrous effect and would destroy the equality we are trying to achieve in Canada for all Canadians.
I want to touch very briefly on some of the developments in the social assistance field. I am pleased to note that a study was undertaken in the province of Nova Scotia of the plight and of the situation of unwed mothers.
What about unwed fathers?

What about unwed fathers? I include unwed fathers too, if they are supporting children, but the point is that when we are speaking about unwed mothers, we are usually speaking about particular situations in which people have become the mothers of children and are not able to care for them. Nobody likes nomenclature which has the effect of casting aspersions on female persons or anybody else in society, but I have important things to say, and I want to communicate them and get a point across. If everybody in the House and across Canada understands what we mean when we say, "an unwed mother", that is good enough for me. When a better terms comes up, I will use it, but right now I am talking about unwed mothers and the fact that services have been provided to them in the past, and I am happy to see that the whole situation is being reviewed and has been reviewed in the province of Nova Scotia. A 325-page study report has been issued entitled "Vulnerable Mothers, Vulnerable Children". I want to point out to my friends to the left in the New Democratic Party, who think they have a monopoly on concern for the people of Canada, that there are other people who are concerned. The government of the province of Nova Scotia is concerned. There are even people in the federal government who are concerned about these problems, and they are doing something about them. They are looking at the situation. As pointed out in that title, "Vulnerable Mothers, Vulnerable Children", we are interested in children. We cannot have
children in this country in need and not being helped and assisted because that would simply mean greater problems down the line, not to mention the humane side of it, which is reason enough. I want hon. members in the New Democratic Party to know that we are aware of these situations. We want to see them dealt with.
There is another point I want to make just to indicate how government policies can have an effect on social services. Recently the Government of Canada indicated it might be cutting back on requirements for eligibility for unemployment insurance. This comes up all the time and plays into the hands of reactionaries who say unemployment insurance is regressive, discourages work, encourages fraud on the government and so forth. That may be so. There certainly are people who are abusing the unemployment insurance program in Canada, but let us not cut off the arm just to remove the lump that causes the disease on the arm. Let us deal with the problem. The government should be careful about changing the criteria of eligibility for unemployment insurance, however, because it could mean that more people would need welfare, and it has been indicated very clearly that the provinces do not have the financial capacity to deal with this.
We owe it to the people of Canada to deal with the problems inherent in the Canada Assistance Plan. It is the instrument that is to be used to deal with very serious problems, and so we should examine it very carefully and try to improve it. We cannot improve the welfare of people by cutting back on necessary services, however. That is the message this party wants to get across, Mr. Speaker. It must be realized that these services are essential not only to the people who receive them but to the nation as a whole. For that reason we all ought to support this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the Canada Assistance Plan and how it can be improved to meet the needs of the people. Like my colleague to my right, I should like to challenge the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) on what I believe was his statement concerning abolishing the Canada Assistance Plan and the federal responsibility for social services. This would be a very serious mistake. Even changing the method of funding to the block method, as is the case with health care services, would be a mistake because there would be less opportunity for the government to make sure that the system is just and equitable for those people who need the service.
I should like to review some of the background of the Canada Assistance Plan, Mr. Speaker. It was developed in 1966 under a federal-provincial agreement, and it can be terminated by any province on one year's notice. The cost of social services is shared 50 per cent by the federal government and 50 per cent by the provinces. I believe that in some cases a province can bill the municipalities for 25 per cent of their share.
In 1980-81, S2.2 billion was spent on social services funded by the Canada Assistance Plan. This provided services for 2.8
February 18, 1982

million poor people in the country or about 12.4 per cent of the population. Just the very poor people in Canada qualify for social services, Mr. Speaker. This includes 639,000 poor families, or one out of every ten families in the country. It also includes 826,000 single people. We know, of course, that many of these are elderly and that many of the elderly are women, so about 31.4 per cent of single people are poor. There is a tremendous need for services in the country, Mr. Speaker, and it is growing every day as a result of lay-offs and unemployment.
When we say $2.2 billion, it sounds like a great deal of money, and of course it is, but a lot of it is used for administration programs and personnel in the social service field. The average welfare cheque for a family of two in British Columbia, a parent and child, is $595 per month. Of this, $300 is used for shelter and $295 for food, fuel, clothing and everything else. Shelter for an average family in Vancouver costs in excess of $300 per month, so little is left for food and the other services that are needed by a family. No matter how we look at it, the level of social assistance falls well below subsistence needs in the country today, and as parliamentarians we must come to grips with this problem.
The National Council on Welfare has stated that last year the poverty level for a single person was $5,928 but Mr. Speaker, the actual welfare payment was only $4,500. For a parent and one child the poverty level was $8,595, yet in my province of British Columbia, in many cases the welfare cheque for that family was less than $7,000. The average income for women last year was $10,860, well below the $25,000 for men.
These figures show that there should be a major review of income support and the welfare system and, of course, the Canada Assistance Plan must be upgraded. We need federal leadership in this field and we need a greater investment of the welfare dollar in the programs of prevention.
I should like to summarize several criticisms of the Canada Assistance Plan including some made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). There are major discrepancies in income support levels and in the access to and quality of social services in different provinces. Some provinces receive less benefit from the Canada Assistance Plan in proportion to their needs than others, particularly the Atlantic provinces. Because a province has to spend a dollar in order to receive a federal dollar and some Atlantic provinces do not have that initial dollar to spend, they are unable to extend services to meet the need which, in many cases, is greater than in other provinces. The CAP guidelines are restrictive and some programs are not fully cost-shared. Some provincial governments could do much more under the guidelines if they accepted their full responsibility. There is a lack of control, accountability and responsibility for federal spending on the program.
In a presentation to the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements task force on the Canada Assistance Plan the minister said that CAP was conceived in the sixties-now we are in the eighties-and asked how the plan can better address the social
Canada Assistance Plan
and economic realities of our time. She said that the level of social aid in almost all the provinces does not lift people over the poverty level; that this is unjust and must be corrected. I should like to know what steps the minister has taken in this regard.
She went on to point out the great inequalities between the different levels of services within the provinces and between the provinces and the federal government. She made the important point that usually the working poor have no place in welfare programs; that they are not included in those which we share and which are strictly for the poor-that is for people who, for one reason or another, are unable to work or are outside the work force or earn very little on a regular basis and, of course, are forced to apply for social assistance. On the broader scale, she said that another problem with CAP is that it does not include, in the usual sense of the word, any equalization, any principle of redistribution; the provinces that are poor have difficulty finding the front-end money to start programs in the first place.
That is what the minister said, and I think we should hold her accountable for making some changes in the directions she mentioned. She should do that or else come and join us in this party and continue to be a more aggressive advocate for change.
I should like to give an example of the negative kind of applications of CAP funds which provinces have been known to introduce. I believe that any changes we make to the Canada Assistance Plan should include some kind of veto system to ensure that 50 per cent of the cost of certain programs which have a negative impact on people, should be disallowed. There should be a method of policing this as far as the provinces are concerned.
1 should like to refer to an example in my province of British Columbia. In October of last year the categories of employables and unemployables were changed by the minister of human resources. Of course, there has always been a rather judgmental and punitive approach to single people on welfare, but it was extended to include single parents with an infant child or two children over the age of 12 years. It was decided by the minister of welfare that the best way to force these unworthy people off the welfare rolls was to cut back on their payments. Of course, jobs were not available, and there were no jobs suitable for mothers with several children who perhaps had never been in the work force or did not have available daycare. Those considerations were ignored, and the welfare payments to those mothers were reduced by $55 per month or $660 per year. It is a punitive provincial policy. There is no way that the federal government and those of us in Parliament should allow Canada Assistance Plan funds to be used in this manner by provinces.
I should like to refer to another example in British Columbia. Recently the minister of human resources reduced funding for rape centres which are extremely important and much needed in various areas of the province. The reason or

February 18, 1982
Canada Assistance Plan
the excuse for cutting back on funds and refusing to fund these essential centres was that the centres would not provide the provincial government with specific personal records. In this case the province really breached the whole concept of confidentiality. It is another reason for the federal government's requiring certain standards in general programs across the land which provinces could not treat in a negative way.
Now I should like to look at our concerns respecting how most of the welfare dollar, or the subsidies through the Canada Assistance Plan covering a range of social services, is geared in almost a negative direction. Most of the social services budget in the provinces is used for what I would call hard core social services which are necessary. They are crisis-oriented. They provide band-aids and, of course, essential financial support. They are very costly services. For example, there is basic income support, but a very high proportion of money goes into institutional care because problems have gone on for too long, families have broken up and other serious problems have developed. Also a very high proportion of the child welfare budget is going to remove children from their homes rather than keeping them there, in which event we are required to pay for very expensive institutional group care or payments to foster parents. In the long run, neither of these do very much to help the persons who are involved. The income support system requires an entire review and major change. The whole question of social assistance should be taken out of the human resources field and integrated with unemployment insurance and various computerized cheques which go out to people. Of course, this would only be the first step toward moving into an integrated system which, hopefully, would become an adequate guaranteed income system. If we took the responsibility for cheques from the social welfare system, those workers could become more involved in the area of prevention.
1 hope the federal government gives active leadership and takes a look at putting some teeth into CAP regulations, so that there will be more emphasis on prevention, self-help and positive support programs to break the welfare cycle, to prevent poverty, and to help people realize their potential in a more positive manner. There should be a much greater investment in self-help programs in local communities, to develop the potential of people and to assist them in developing their own community services. There should be more investment in training and in paraprofessional service roles. For example, we could use people in the communities, many of whom have experienced poverty. There should be programs to strengthen families and to keep children in their homes. We should think of the number of young teenage mothers at the present time. This number has increased at a critical rate during the past few years. If ever they required help and support from the community, indeed it is now; it is very much a priority. We must become involved while they are young and before their young children are damaged. We should provide support in health and educational opportunities as well as needed job training. Also, we should think about the working poor who are struggling, some of whom have large families, to survive on barely minimum wages. We should provide them with a
system wherein they could retain their independence and receive some help with the provision of daycare or supplements to their family income, in order to prevent them from saying that it is much easier to go on welfare than to keep working. It is not easier on welfare, but certainly it is not easy to work at low wages with a family. We must become serious about what 1 would call social investments, which will prove less costly in the long run.
1 should like to refer to a specific example concerning people who live in a public housing neighbourhood in my riding. This is what I would call a community development program. The Canada Assistance Plan has a category for community development, but I challenge someone to show me how many provinces are actually using it. This is the type of thing we must stress. We must build on the strength of people and open up opportunities in local communities. The example to which I refer is a movement started close to ten years ago by some mothers on welfare. They refused to be regarded as victims or second-class citizens. They insisted on their rights, rather than being just passive recipients caught up in the welfare cycle. They organized and participated in a lot of local action activities on behalf of their children. Then they began to think of ways in which they could expand as a co-operative community in order to provide their own services, to train their own people, and to heck with the welfare department. They felt that they had many talents and could do many things themselves, and they soon proved it. First, they organized a food co-operative in which they used a lot of their own people. They trained some of them who gained expertise and developed new skills. Along with some mothers in other housing projects, they convinced the minister of human resources to provide what they called an opportunities allowance of an extra $100 per month to do community work in the interests of their own communities. Also they helped to develop daycare and childcare services. They developed the concept of a co-operative community. They realized that if they could establish a food co-operative, the same could be done for various services. Thus they received a three-year LEAP grant, which is the kind of grant that should be available through the Canada Assistance Plan. In this case they received it from the old Canada manpower department. They trained some of their people in child care and developed daycare centres. Other people were trained in providing services for senior citizens and have gone on to work as homemakers in paid capacities. Eventually they obtained their own building, into which they moved their services. It was operated by a local board and they hired as many people from the community as possible. They introduced special pre-employment training programs, of which quite a number of Indian women who had no job experience took advantage.

All show and no substance, Mr. Speaker. Let us look at the motion and see where we are on the "unfair and unnecessary burden of high gasoline prices". The price of gasoline has increased by 75 cents. That is what this Liberal government did with the help of the NDP, this party of principle. Higher fuel oil prices is what we have today. Unemployment at an all-time record high is what we have today. All this because the NDP, the party of principle, supported the government in a mealy-mouthed way because they thought they could gain seats. They are a party of principle only if they can gain seats.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to speak about the budget as it relates to the borrowing bill. The money borrowed to run the government affects every area of our economy. It is spent in every department. Let us look at what happens. In 1980 our economy experienced zero growth, the worst performance in 26 years. Productivity fell by V/2 per cent and housing starts fell to their lowest level in 13 years. While the first half of 1981 saw reasonably healthy economic growth, the economy is now in severe recession. Severe recession? It is moving toward a depression of unparalleled proportions, something we in this country have never seen before. What has the government continually been told, Mr. Speaker? In October, Statistics Canada warned as follows:
Signs that a slowdown in economic activity will extend over the second half of 1981 proliferated in July as the Canadian composite leading indicator fell for the second consecutive month, and the weakness that characterized several components in June broadened and intensified in July.
Six days before the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) brought in his budget, Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada said this on November 6, 1981:
-market slowdown in activity could develop into a recession during the coming months. The sharp decline in indicators of economic activity has already led firms to cut production, and lay-offs have become widespread.
February 18, 1982

Again on December 7, 1981, Statistics Canada said this:
The third quarter downturn of real GNP will not be reversed in the near future. The index and its components indicate that the negative forces accumulating in the economy continued to spread and intensify. The outlook for all major components of final demand remains dim.
That was when the Minister of Finance was contemplating changes in his anti-growth budget, a budget which was stifling initiative in Canada. Statistics Canada was saying, in other words, that unemployment is going to get worse; bankruptcies are going to become commonplace; farmers are not going to get the prices they need for their commodities and will go under; small businessmen are going to suffer and go out of business; the young people coming out of our universities and technical colleges have absolutely nothing to look forward to in the form of jobs because there are none. All this because of the budget and the national energy policy proposed and implemented by the government. This is what they said as recently as last month:
-the marked slowdown in the economy currently under way will not likely be reversed for the first quarter of 1982.
In other words, there is not a hope unless the government does something by the end of March, 1982. It goes on:
The filtered composite index fell 2.6% in October, one of the largest declines since the 1975 recession. The downturn was generalized among all the components, including those,... which have the longest leads in signaling a turning point. .. . the weakness in the manufacturing sector broadened in reaction to the slackening of final demand.... the speed of descent will not be substantially attenuated before the end of this quarter.
There is not a great deal of hope that it will be stopped then. Well, I can go on and on. Certainly we know what they have done. They are ruining our economy, a system where men and women could look around and say: "1 can do." We in Canada were blessed by God Almighty with an abundance of resources. We have an abundance of fresh water, an abundance of people who have the foresight and drive to go out and do something, to say "I am going to do it." But we have not been blessed with a type of government which recognizes that in the Canadian people. Over the past 14 years, we have not been blessed with a kind of government which recognizes the freedom of the individual, allowing that individual to proceed on his own, allowing him to take the risks, allowing him to work and save, and thereby contribute to the growth of the country. Instead, we have had a government which has very systematically stated, "We will intervene in the economy. We will control the economy. We will do it in such a way." The government then starts using phrases such as, "It is for the people of Canada." Well, are the risk-takers not the people of Canada? Are those who want to go out and build something with their own two hands not the people of Canada? No, no.
It reminds me of the story, which 1 am sure all hon. members of the House have heard, about the little red hen baking the bread. Finally, after all the interventions and all the government interference, it sits on the fence and crows away. Everyone wonders, why does this little hen not bake any bread now? No one is baking bread. Why? That is what is happening.

the type of agreement, did eventually sign. He looked at Canada and realized that we had to get the economic wheels going again. It is my view that he was willing to sacrifice something to get that to happen. However, it did not happen and is not happening. We have unlimited numbers of small businesses in the oil patch, and the western basin going out of business.
The members of the NDP alluded to the separatist vote. We even had one member cross the floor before this evening's session suggesting that we were not doing our job in Alberta because in a provincial byelection we allowed a separatist to be elected. 1 say to those across the way that we are trying to do our job. However, we cannot do our job and fight Liberals and stupid Liberal policies at the same time.
That is a clear warning. I know some of those people who voted. They would have voted for the Western Canada Concept, not because they do not love their country and not because they do not see the blessings this country has from God Almighty who looked down upon our country, blessed us with resources and gave us people with initiative. These are the people who dirtied their hands. They broke the soil and built something with their own hands so that when they leave this world, they will have something to pass on to their children.
This government with its energy policy and budget is stifling that kind of initiative. It sickens me to sit here and listen to the tripe that we get day by day from the government benches about what they are going to do, how they are going to make the economy go again, how they are going to stimulate the economy and create jobs. My God, all you have to do is to leave people alone, get out of their daily lives, and allow them to do the work they want to do.
I talk daily to men who want to accomplish something. They are willing to work 14, 16, 18 hours a day in order to build something. They are being stifled by the government. How in God's name can someone start a business today with interest rates on borrowed money running around 20 per cent? That is the rate on a normal bank loan. How in God's name can anyone get a Small Business Development Bond? They are only available for businesses in dire straits. Imagine a direct government policy not to help healthy small businesses develop through the Small Business Development Bond. We are not going to help a small enterprise grow and create jobs through this bond. Only those in dire straits, those going belly-up are going to be helped. My goodness, it defies logic.
Today, the second anniversary of their election, the Liberal members walked into this chamber wearing red carnations. Believe me, I would have been happy to wear a red carnation today had this government brought in policies recognizing the need to encourage development of the individual so that by his sweat, tears and dirty hands he can build a business which he can pass on to his children.
I would have been happy to wear a red carnation had I not read in the paper today that housing starts are at an all-time low and, for the first time in Canada in 25 years, people are having to double up. Young people getting married today cannot look to the future in the same way as those who

married ten or 15 years ago. They knew that if they worked hard some day they could own their own homes. What is happening now? These young married couples must now live at home with mother and father, they must live with their in-laws. That is no kind of future for our children.
I would have been glad to wear a red carnation today if the unemployment rate were at a tolerable level. We talk about the unemployment rale reaching 9 per cent. There are over a million people unemployed in Canada. There is no need for that with our abundance of resources. We have the technology, understanding and desire to get this country moving.
I would have worn a red carnation today had this government shown that it is willing to cut back on the expenditures it is making daily. The spending of the government is out of hand. It prints money like it is going out of style. The government is growing.
Every time the government makes an announcement, it costs the people of Canada another half a million dollars. What is that with a deficit of $17 billion? A billion dollars staggers me. I have no way of comprehending what it is. All I know is that the people of Canada are carrying this burden on their backs. They are frightened.
People right across this country from British Columbia to Newfoundland are frightened about the erosion in their standard of living, their opportunity to make a living, the future for themselves and their children. Can you imagine that in our Canada which is blessed with an abundance of resources? Our Canada has the kind of people who want to accomplish something.
There is no reason for the situation we are in today. We do not have to track U.S. interest rates. We do not have to confiscate through the national energy policy in the name of so-called Canadianization. All we have to do is to encourage Canadians to go out and buy, work and take over some of the oil industry that is here. Will that Canadianize it? That is not Canadianizing. It is not one man taking steps to become an owner.
It is my hope that my remarks tonight will cause some members to think. 1 hope it will help some members to talk to their constituents and help encourage members to visit an unemployment insurance office to ask those people who are unemployed the most resounding question which is most often asked-why? They are not blaming anyone; they are just asking why this is happening in Canada, a country with the great wealth and population we have. How can the government allow this to happen? The answer is there, Mr. Speaker, if we are willing to take the time to find it.
I would suggest to the Liberal government that if it allowed members of the House, for even half a day, to participate equally with them in drafting a policy to attack the economy, they would be astounded at the results. I do not believe for one moment that all the talent in the House is in the Conservative ranks. I am sure the New Democratic Party believes that all the talent is in its corner. They do have some talent, and there

is considerable talent on the Liberal side. There is all this talent sitting in the House of Commons while the government is being run by a close-knit, select few.
I have participated in committees and 1 have tried to have some input on the national energy policy when the bill was in committee, I do not have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, because you have been here longer than I, that it is useless. One sits in those committees, which are mainly composed of government members and, in most cases, are chaired by a government member. It is a process whereby if there is any possibility that they might lose a vote in committee, the government members leave the room in order to destroy the quorum so that a vote cannot be taken. Opposition members who go into committee try their best to have the government at least attempt to change legislation and alleviate the impact it might have on people. However, it is an exercise in futility.
During the two years that I have been here, the only committee which I have seen make any progress was the constitutional committee. It was held in the open, in front of television cameras for all Canadians to see. Canadians could see positive suggestions being made and who was making them. It did not matter who was making these suggestions because we were working as a group. This would never have been accomplished had we not fillibustered in the House. What a waste!
I would like to give my opinion on an issue which I feel is very urgent. It is the byelection in Olds-Didsbury in southern Alberta where a member of the Western Canada Concept was elected. To my knowledge, it is the first time that an avowed separatist candidate will be sitting in the Alberta legislature. This alarms me. 1 am alarmed that people whom I know, including some of my relatives, who live in the Olds-Didsbury area may have voted for the Western Canada Concept. In other words, they are saying that there is no use. They have tried, they have signalled Ottawa time and again that it is not allowing them to do what they want. But the bureaucrats and politicians in Ottawa do not understand what is happening in Alberta, and indeed in western Canada.
I will not get into the argument of whether they have been treated poorly in the past. I will not get into the argument of whether the westerner is being treated badly. All that I am saying is that there is a very clear perception in southern Alberta that, according to the government here in Ottawa, Canada is made up of Quebec and Ontario. When one sees the VIA Rail cuts and the attack on the Crow rate, there is no other conclusion to which they can come.
I believe that we must revise the Senate in order to provide the representation which this country deserves before it is too late. The Senate should be reformed to allow perhaps ten elected senators from each province so that our upper chamber will have an input into our government. We must put a ceiling on the number of members who will come into the House of Commons. We must make provisions which would allow members of the House of Commons to participate more actively in government policy making. As the situation exists now, 1 am here to represent my constituency of Athabasca, but my job in
sitting in the opposition is to oppose everything the government introduces. I am sure if I had some input into the drafting of government legislation-even just to give ideas-we could all work much better and provide a more positive view of Canada and its economic direction.
It is my plea to all members of the House that there is talent on all sides of the House and we must all sit down together to attack the most threatening problem facing Canada today, namely, the state of emergency of our economy, before riots break out in the streets and our country destroys itself.

Canadians are today self-sufficient in all forms of energy but one. We are self-sufficient in coal, in hydroelectricity, in uranium and in natural gas as well as various renewable forms of energy. In the past year, a number of Canadian companies that were facing gas surpluses in this country were attracted to the United States in the hope of achieving success in that market. They were encouraged by the rate of success in exploratory wells there and by world level prices. Many of those companies are now returning to Canada, having experienced high interest rates, poor economic conditions and disappointing drilling results. The situation, in short, is rather different today. An extensive report in The Calgary Herald a few days ago noted that many of the companies that had plunged into the United States have begun to return to Canada.
The Canadianization element of the National Energy Program has been discussed today. This element, as any public opinion poll will indicate, has the broad support of the Canadian people. I should like to spend a moment noting the progress that has been made in this area.
Since the National Energy Program was announced in October, 1980, ten Canadian companies have acquired foreign companies worth more than $100 million each. In total, more than $6 billion has been spent in acquiring previously foreign held oil and gas assets. The vast majority of those deals, contrary to what some people have alleged, were private sector deals. They were not government deals, not nationalization but Canadianization. Of course, there were two exceptions-the Petro-Canada acquisition of Petrofina and the 25 per cent share in Suncor acquired by the Ontario government. All the acquisitions since the announcement of the National Energy Program have contributed to increasing Canadian ownership of upstream production revenues by about 6.3 percentage points. According to Petroleum Monitoring Agency data, to which several references have been made today, the level of foreign ownership of production revenues was 72 per cent in 1980. As of the middle of last month, this figure declined to 65.7 per cent. Those statistics indicate the degree to which there has been a marked change of ownership in the petroleum industry within the last 18 months. I am quite confident that we shall achieve our goal of 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry by 1990.
In discussing the success of the Canadianization program, and against the background of allegations that somehow the program was engaged in nationalization as distinct from Canadianization, or was a government take-over as distinct from a private sector venture, I want to note that not only have there been both private and public sector ventures, but the government recently concluded an agreement with co-operatives in Canada to form new oil and gas ventures. The Cooperative Energy Corporation and the Co-operative Energy Development Corporation provide the opportunity for literally millions of Canadians to participate in their own oil industry. This opportunity has been limited to more restricted numbers of Canadians in the past. For the first time, partly through the vehicle of the new Co-operative Energy Corporation, many more Canadians will have the opportunity to participate in an enterprise which has been closed to them in the past.

Additional to the acquisition route and the new venture route upon which I have briefly touched, there is another way in which Canadianization in the petroleum industry is going forward, that is, farm-ins by Canadian companies with foreign-controlled corporations. We have seen a number of such farm-in arrangements in recent months. 1 refer the House to the Alberta Energy Corporation, the state enterprise of Alberta, which arranged a farm-in of Gulf Canada lands in western Canada. More recently, both Imperial Oil and Texaco have not only agreed upon farm-ins with various Canadian companies but have repeatedly indicated their interest in additional farm-ins, so as to qualify for the higher incentive grant.
We have had some discussion during this debate about the borrowing authority as to energy prices and fairness. It is our contention that, in the first instance, fairness was introduced in the National Energy Program by the grants which are available to all Canadians to participate in conservation. This route was not open before to those who did not have the resources to make necessary changes to their dwellings or in some cases to their vehicles. Now they have the opportunity to gain the benefits of conservation.
Beyond that example of fairness is, of course, the price agreement reached with the government of Alberta under which the refinery cost of crude oil at Toronto in 1984 will be $52 per barrel. Under the budget of the previous government, the price would have been about $58 per barrel, even under a moderate international price increase projection.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate you on your duties in the chair tonight. It is always pleasing to see the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) in the chair.
Bill C-93 implements a number of commitments made to energy producing provinces, provides several technical changes in the federal excise tax system, and seeks to obtain new borrowing powers for the fiscal year 1982-83. In the first part, the government is seeking borrowing authority for $6.6 billion, and this borrowing authority is directly connected with the budget. In light of the current economic situation, I agree with the minister that a review of the budget's objectives is important to provide a background for evaluating the merits of the bill.
In the budget, the government correctly identified rapidly rising inflation as the main problem in the country. Inflation pushes up interest rates, destroys investor confidence and generally slows down economic activity. In turn, this leads to a number of problems such as rising unemployment, erosionsQf real income, and borrowers saddled with the burden of ever-increasing interest rates. In Canada this has been marked by a period of stagflation in which the economy has been stagnant but inflation has continued to accelerate. In dealing solely with the problems of inflation, the government has failed to come to grips also with the problem of unemployment. The government appears to have failed to realize that there are two problems facing Canada and that each of them can be addressed at the same time.
To do this we need policies to restore the level of confidence in our country that will encourage Canadians and non-Canadians to invest in Canada. We must create a climate in which creative and courageous men and women may take risks and realize rewards. We must ensure that the public interest shall be preserved and that both the strong and the weak shall have equal opportunities. The great need at the present time is to build a property-owning democracy where not only do conditions encourage the individual to own the home in which he dwells and the farm fields he cultivates, but in addition allow him to save sufficient income to share in the ownership of the social and industrial future of this great country.
We must embark on a national development policy that will strengthen all areas. Canadians of all groups and regions must have equal opportunities to share in the national prosperity.
This involves an investment, not a mere spending, and the distinction between those two elements is one of the basic concepts that has escaped this government and that has been brought to the attention of the government, not only by myself but by one of the speakers on my left who spoke in this debate earlier.
Canada is one of the most beautiful and blessed of nations, and Canadians have the right, the obligation, and should be given the opportunity to create the world's finest society. It is important that the Foreign Investment Review Act and the capital gains tax be re-evaluated in light of our great need to attract investment in our country. By doing so this will revive our dollar and give us the flexibility to drop interest rates to the level they should be so we can get Canada moving forward again.
To do this we have to maximize the involvement of the private sector because small Canadian business employs more Canadians than any other sector of our economy. We have also to get on with the megaprojects and use them as development tools in all parts of our country.
We have a crisis in housing caused by high interest rates. The Clark government program to permit deductions of mortgage interest and property taxes from income tax, which was opposed by the Liberal and New Democratic parties, was then and is now the right measure to stimulate home building and the building materials industries in Canada today.
If ever there was a time when all governments in the country should be moving in the same direction, it is now. At this moment, federal-provincial relations are probably at an alltime low, with the federal government avoiding cost-sharing programs and local expertise and electing to take unilateral action to dissolve the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and to do its own thing in the development of areas that suffer from regional disparity.
The budget failed to recognize the tremendous importance and the potential of research and development in this country. The high technology industries have become the winners in today's economy. Our government has failed to follow the lead of these enlightened corporations. It has not stimulated industrial research nor has it regained lost markets. It has not moved into new ones nor expanded the great export potential of our country, which is so rich in terms of its natural resources and its educated population.
The budget should have allowed a reduction in taxable income by the excess interest that people are paying who have had to renew their mortgages. It should have allowed farmers a tax credit for the interest paid for seed and fertilizer. It should have allowed the small-business man to pay interest only on his long-term borrowings for at least a year. It should have allowed normal depreciation for new purchases or even accelerated the depreciation.
With huge revenues from the oil pricing agreements starting to flow into federal coffers, we have a rare opportunity to attack our deficit position and our accumulating deficit and at the same time to invest in the development of Canada. We
February 18, 1982

have to maximize our benefits from megaprojects, develop our natural resources, such as forestry, fisheries and agriculture. We have to update our creaking transport system and modernize our ports so that we can move more readily into export markets.
Shrinking space availability on ships registered under flags of convenience calls for an urgent evaluation of the merits of a Canadian merchant marine.
Hand in hand with an industrial strategy to bring about the economic recovery of our nation go training programs to enable Canadians to avail themselves of these opportunities.
It was just 24 months ago that the Liberal Party was elected nationally on a platform that higher energy policies were unnecessary and that they could manage the economy better than the Clark government. Now, 60 to 80 cents a gallon later, people are beginning to recall that during the Clark government inflation remained stable, jobs were being created at the rate of 30,000 a month and that purchasing power of wages rose. Under the self-proclaimed economic miracle workers now in office we have seen 30-year record level of unemployment and inflation, a decline in real wages, the biggest tax burden since the war, the gutting of the passenger rail system and proposals to reduce the financial commitment of the Liberal government to equalization, health and post-secondary education.
One of the crudest things about the current budget is that it penalizes Canadians who are trying to provide for their future and their families. It appears to penalize Canadians who adopt the noble and important concept of providing for the severely disruptive financial burden caused by unexpected dental or medical bills and incapacity due to illness.
It also penalizes the Canadian breadwinner who attempts to provide for himself and his dependants on retirement and after his demise. I am speaking again of the serious retrogressive step being taken by the government in taxing life insurance, dental and medical plans. In my opinion, this is a cruel and merciless tax grab that can cost the government more in social justice payments and unemployment insurance than it can hope to gain from these measures.
I do not often speculate about the future, but 1 do try to learn from the past. One of the things that I learned early on in Parliament was to read the budget papers that are filed with the budget. The Department of Finance analysis of the federal tax expenditures for individuals, which was tabled as one of the budget papers accompanying the November, 1981 budget, identified provisions of the tax system that in effect exclude certain types of income from tax, and the authors of the paper refer to these as tax expenditures because their economic effect makes them equivalent to spending programs.
In his budget speech of October 28, 1980, the minister noted that tax expenditures are expensive and it is incumbent on government to ensure that the incentives are effective and costs justified. In a prophetic statement, he went on to add that he wondered whether the economy might not be better
Taxation
served by a tax system with lower rates but with fewer and more selective incentives.
The paper tabled in the House describes tax expenditures as being composed of four different types. The first category includes cases where certain kinds of income are excluded. Examples are one half of capital gains, the full gain realized on the sale of principal residences, and various employment benefits, including interest free or low interest loans from employers. In this same category is included imputed rent on owner-occupied dwellings. That is right. The bureaucrats in the ivory towers of finance have identified the fact that Canadians living in the homes which they own pay no rent, and they feel that this is in fact a tax expenditure.
There are others. The second category deals with deduction tax expenditures and includes unemployment insurance contributions, tuition fees, gifts to the Crown, charitable donations, etc. Exemption tax expenditures include such things as married exemption and exemption for wholly dependent children. Tax credits tax expenditures is the final category and it includes refundable income tested child tax credits and tax credits for investment in machinery and equipment and buildings in certain sectors. I have by no means attempted to identify the very large number of tax expenditures which are discussed in the paper, but rather to attempt to identify the subject matter. Why is it important? It is important because it gives us an idea of the thinking of the senior bureaucrats in the finance department who are charged with the responsibility of making tax proposals to their minister. The November 1981 budget affected nine tax expenditures mentioned in this paper.
The paper admits that many of the tax expenditures serve important policy objectives and do so in an effective manner. It goes on to say that while some may wish that the budget had gone further in the direction of removing tax expenditures and lowering tax rates, it has to be recognized that any changes in tax expenditures must be part of an ongoing process of evaluation and review. It takes into account the prevailing economic circumstances and the capacity of the tax system to deal with large-scale changes. The paper admits that the existence of tax expenditures is important, but it also adds that for some purposes the tax system is a legitimate tool with which to address social and economic goals. In my opinion the ownership of one's home free of imputed rent is a worth-while social goal, and so too is the attempt of Canadians to provide for their dependants through life insurance and medical and dental plans. Tax exemptions for wives and children, tax credits to encourage industries to locate and provide jobs in areas that suffer from regional disparity and exemptions for those over 65 are all measures that are worthwhile and have grown up with our tax system.
I have no quarrel with government departments studying these tax expenditures, reviewing and evaluating them. My concern is that we have to be very much aware that many of the things we value highly and have come to take for granted are being examined by many of the people who have already

identified some of the measures and convinced their minister to propose their elimination in his recent budget. It was an aroused opposition and an aroused Canadian public that forced the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to change his mind on some of these proposals, and we witnessed the spectacle of his public retreat. We are now witnessing a very significant delay by the minister on some of the other measures which are repugnant to a large number of Canadians.
