speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken on budget bills, particularly borrowing bills, many times in the House and 1 do not recall, in the nearly ten years 1 have been here, a borrowing bill on which there were two Conservative speakers in a row who really did not condemn us very strongly for borrowing money. It strikes me as being a very strange phenomenon, and I think perhaps the reason for it is that the money the government is seeking to borrow in the next fiscal year is considerably less than the authority given for the last fiscal year. In the last fiscal year we had authority to borrow something in the order of $14 billion, and of course it must be understood that the authority does not mean you borrow that much. It looks as if we will have borrowed about $12 billion of the $14 billion. This year the authority allows for about $6.6 billion, and given the $2 billion left over, we will be borrowing something less than $9 billion. That is the anticipation. So we can see that the
borrowing authority in this bill is for about $5 billion less than last year.
Now I think it is fitting that we periodically have borrowing bills in the House. Usually it is once a year, but it has been more often when the government requires supplementary borrowing. This, of course, is in contrast with the United States where Congress puts an absolute limit on the national debt and the government can borrow up to that limit. In Canada, when we have to borrow additional sums, the government has to come to Parliament for approval. I think that is a worth-while activity and gives us a chance to debate how the money is spent, the merits or demerits of deficits and their size.
I think I would like to deal with two problems which are usually raised by more conservative speakers with regard to government indebtedness, expenditures and so on. The first, of course, is that government spending is wasteful. It is throwing money away and has a negative impact on the economy. The other is that almost all inflation stems from government spending. Those are the two myths which cloud the conservative mind.
First, I would like to deal with the nature of government spending. There are basically two areas where all governments spend their money. One is on the actual operations of government itself. In Canada, this accounts for roughly one third of all federal government expenditures, going for such things as the post office, national defence, and so on. The vast majority, two thirds of government expenditures, is in the area of what would be called transfers. These are transfers to the people in the form of pensions, family allowances, welfare and so forth. These are transfers to the provinces which, in turn, transfer the money to people and also pay their own costs of operation. They are transfers in terms of paying off debts, again to people. 1 think we should clearly understand the difference between those kinds of expenditures because it is the first expenditure, the cost of operating the government, that actually takes away from the economy of the country. It is the expenditure which takes goods and services out of the economy which could be used, otherwise.
The second category, the transfers, are moneys which are taken from one pocket and put into another pocket, with no net loss in between. The net costs are the costs of providing the service, and that is included in the first category. I think it is good that we understand this and that we look at these two kinds of expenditures.
1 would first like to look at the transfer side, because it is a side which provides two thirds of the expenditures of the federal government.
I would particularly like to deal with one very current aspect, and that is the aspect of the transfers to the provinces and, in turn, to the municipalities. This is an area I think we should really consider. The transfers to the provinces in the year 1981-82 will amount to a little over $13 billion. Also, the transfer of tax points, which was done in the last few years, adds up to something a little over $18 billion. That is, almost
February 18, 1982

one third of all the money that the federal government spends goes to the provinces. We should look at the nature of this transfer and the growth of the transfers themselves.
In 1959, the Government of Canada transferred $0.6 billion, or roughly $600 million, to the provinces. The figure which appears in the chart that I have, although it has gone up considerably since then, shows that it rose to $11.8 billion in 1979, which amounted to a 2,000 per cent increase, or 20 times as much. There are all kinds of factors there; but the fact is that the amount of money which was transferred from the federal government to the provinces in that period of time increased by 20 times. If one compares the growth of federal revenues with that of provincial revenues in that period of time, one finds that federal revenues rose from $5.8 billion to $43.5 billion, or an increase by seven and a half times. The transfers from the federal government to the provinces tripled, or grew three times as fast as the revenue of the federal government. Therefore, we see a significant shift from the federal government to the provinces. That is very significant when we talk about federal deficits and about the way we organize things in this country.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) speaks of his concern about the degree of this transfer, of his concern about the amount of money which is going from federal coffers to the provinces, and when he says we must keep this under some control, he is referring to the fact that those transfers have increased at almost three times the rate of the revenue in the federal government.
Let us look at the revenues of the federal government itself and of the provincial governments when we are dealing in terms of these transfers. In 1959, the Government of Canada had received approximately 52 per cent of all revenues in this country. The provinces and the municipalities received 48 per cent, which was very close to half and half. Half the money went to the federal government and half went to the provinces. It was very close.
Let us look at it in 1979, again which reveals the situation. By 1959, the amount of all government revenues had declined from 52 per cent to 33 per cent. It went from one half to one third of all revenues going to governments in this country. The provincial and municipal revenues rose from 48 per cent, again roughly half, to 67 per cent or two thirds. Therefore, we see this tremendous shift. From a point where federal and provincial revenues were almost 50-50, it went to the point where the revenues to the federal government amounted to roughly one third of all government revenues, and the provincial revenues amounted to two thirds.
1 am not decrying this situation. There is a lot of logic to it. One of the very substantial reasons that provincial government revenues increased over this period was that we expanded our educational institutions considerably. In the latter part of the period, we expanded our medical and hospital facilities even more. These were two of the very large pieces in the extension of revenue.
It is extremely important that the revenue situation be understood by those who claim the federal government is
Taxation
destroying this country because it is taking so much out. In the beginning, I said that I wanted to speak about the two major classifications of expenditures of the federal government, the one being the expenditures on goods and services, or operations of government itself, and the other being the transfer to people in provinces and so on. I dealt with the second one.
1 would like to deal with the first one for just a moment because it is important that we take a look at how extensive this is before we condemn government expenditures as being the great crime of our time. Again, I have a chart which illustrates expenditures from about 1953 to 1979. I would like to deal with what is called government expenditures on goods and services; that is, the operation of the government. This chart deals with the government expenditures as a percentage of the gross national product. We see that all government expenditures, as a percentage of gross national product, in current prices, rose from 1953, when it was about 17 per cent or 18 per cent, to approximately 24 per cent by 1978. There was a substantial increase of the portion of the gross national product. What really counts is what governments take away from the economy for goods and services, not transfers. When we break this down, we see quite a different picture if we consider what the federal government's expenditures were in terms of the gross national product, or goods and services. In 1953, the federal government spent approximately 10 per cent of the gross national product on goods and services. I am talking about the post office, national defence spending, the whole business. By 1978, the federal portion had dropped to about 6 per cent of the gross national product. When 1 look at these figures, I find it hard to believe that the great enemy of the people, our economy, our growth and what makes Canada work is federal government expenditures. That has not increased. It has decreased in terms of the GNP.

1 would now like to deal more in generalities. I believe 1 have put to rest two myths. One is that government expenditure is terribly wasteful, that the government is throwing money away. The other is that government debt is the cause of all inflation.
There is a more prevalent myth which affects the whole economic world at this point. It is what I call the myth of macroeconomic activity or action, solving problems today the way they were solved in the Keynesian era. I do not think that will work. Those monetary policies will not work. 1 do not believe a reduction of the money supply, increased rates and so on, are having the effects that we had hoped for. On the other hand, I do not think lower taxes and attempts to increase the fiscal means to meet increased demand will work either. There are all kinds of reasons for this. I do not have time to give them now. I would like to continue the next time this debate resumes.
I think we are all satisfied that the monetary policy is not working well. One reason is the side effects it creates. High interest rates are inflationary. A figure was given to me. I will have to qualify it a bit. If the exchange rate was the same as it was in 1975, the additional cost to this country for imports would be about S12 billion a year. Let us go to the other side, the one which the NDP praises. Their notion is that by lowering taxes and thereby circulating more money, demand is increased, which really tends to be inflationary. It would not have the effect it used to have. The money goes into savings, luxury goods from foreign sources rather than creating the desired effects. We have to look away from macroeconomics and look at micro, although I do not like that term. We have to look at inflation in terms of

subtopic: AIR CANADA-(A) MANDATORY RETIREMENT AGE (B) REQUEST THAT PILOT BE REINSTATED
AIR CANADA-(A) MANDATORY RETIREMENT AGE (B) REQUEST THAT PILOT BE REINSTATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the risk of being labelled a one-issue member, I again rise on a matter of human rights.
It is now almost two years since I first began protesting and urging the government and members of this House to take all possible action to eliminate the discriminating practices of mandatory retirement which exist in Canada; practices which, needless to say, are denying many Canadians their right to work and contribute to the general wellbeing of our country.
At this point I do point out that, as mentioned, I have already spoken on this troubling concern on several occasions. My views are well recorded in Hansard. However, I will take this opportunity to express some further concerns as a result of my question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on February 11, 1982, regarding an order in council ordering Air Canada to reinstate Captain Ross Stevenson to his original position as an airline pilot.
As numerous members of the House are aware, the Supreme Court of Canada has recently ruled unanimously that Ontario municipalities cannot impose a mandatory retirement age of 60 on their firefighters, even if that had been negotiated into their collective agreement.
Considering this fact and considering the fact that this case is identical to the case of Captain Ross Stevenson, an Air
February 18, 1982

Canada pilot who was forced to retire because of the collective agreement between the Canadian Airline Pilots Association and Air Canada, there remains no doubt in my mind that the minister should introduce an order in council designed to reinstate Captain Ross Stevenson with Air Canada.
Granted, I can understand the Minister of Transport wanting to leave the decision to the union and the company involved, but 1 cannot understand how the minister can allow a double standard to exist among different groups of workers. This is clearly a time for leadership and the minister should be leading the way for equality within our system. Are we, as members of the House, to ignore that a discriminatory practice exists? I say no to this practice which denies to the individual a healthy self-image as a result of being actively involved in the work force.
The fundamental problem and main obstacle to equality for federal employees is Section 14(c) of the Canadian Human Rights Act which permits age discrimination and denies some Crown corporation employees the right to work beyond 60 years of age. Why is it not possible for all Canadians to work past 60 if they are capable and want to, especially when some are permitted to? Why should the others be discriminated against?
The Canadian Human Rights Act, Section 14(c), is preventing federal employees of Crown corporations from continuing their employment past what is called the normal retirement age. Why are we, as members of the House, allowing this cruel game of semantics to continue within our legal system? Are we not elected here to serve the Canadian people with equality and without discrimination?
Captain Ross Stevenson is a victim of this "fixed" game and three times now he has gone to court to change the rules of Section 14(c) to remove the discrimination which exists; spending thousands of his retirement dollars. Why should Mr. Stevenson be spending his money to do a job which is our responsibility? That responsibility is providing a non-discriminatory system of social justice. This policy of placing thousands of our productive work force "on the shelf' is not only expensive and wasteful, but extremely unjust.
It is morally wrong to reject efficient and willing workers because of their date of birth. All that is required is to delete Section 14(c) from the Canadian Human Rights Act, as recommended two years ago by both Senator Croll's special senate committee on retirement age policies and by the Canadian Human Rights Commission. It is on this note that I urge the House to bring equality to our system by deleting Section 14(c), and to put an end to the cruel semantics game of "normal retirement age" within our legal system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it should be interesting to hear what the parliamentary secretary has to say in response to my questions. My question was a very simple one, asking for three memos. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) took part in a decision to give jobs to Japanese and not to Canadians. 1 do not think that is the policy of this government, but it almost has to be, since that is the only motivation 1 can see.
The only company in the world which to date has made the type of equipment required for the Ridley Terminals Incorporated stacker-reclaimers at Ridley Island near Prince Rupert is Stephens-Adamson. We understand that company's bid was $1 million lower than that of the Japanese. Its delivery date was two months earlier. The minister says time is of the essence. The delivery could still beat that of the Japanese, even if Stephens-Adamson was given the order today.
Finally, with respect to guarantees in relation to technology and quality, at Westshore Terminals some years ago Stephens-Adamson was asked to guarantee a piece of equipment. The company gave a guarantee. There has been only one fault in that piece of equipment since and that was three years after the Five-year guarantee period.
1 am asking for three memos. Two are from the National Harbours Board. The first one, frankly, is full of falsehoods, and that is the reason I want to have a look at it, and the

February 18, 1982
Adjournment Debate
second is an internal memo. These memos have to do with the decision by Ridley Terminals to buy this Japanese equipment.
Ridley Terminals was created in December of 1981 after two years of playing around, trying to get this job under way.
I know that a letter of intent was given to the Japanese firm at least a week before the board of Ridley Terminals met to consider this decision. I sounds to me as if the intention was to give the contract to the Japanese from the beginning. I have been putting pressure on the minister for some six weeks about this matter, Mr. Speaker, and I suggest to you it is only because I upset the plans that the letting of the contract was delayed for two and a half to three weeks. 1 should like to see it delayed even further.
The second item I want to deal with is the point made by the minister in his answer when 1 put the question regarding the memos. The minister said he had directed that the National Harbours Board should meet with the company to give a full explanation of the decision. That was just not done, Mr. Speaker.
I have a copy of a telex sent to the minister today in which the company says it had been informed of the arrangement to have the meeting, by his office, and had subsequently arranged a meeting in Vancouver on February 8 with the vice-chairman of the National Harbours Board, the acting chairman of Ridley Terminals, and the president of Swan Wooster, which is the engineering consulting company involved, before a full review meeting on February 9. The telex says that they were shocked when the meeting was refused, and more astonishing was that the offer to meet with them was on the condition that they would not use any information to pursue further evaluation. They state that they could not agree to this condition.
All i am looking for is three memos, Mr. Speaker. If the minister or his parliamentary secretary can convince me and Stephens-Adamson that in fact there was a fair evaluation of this contract, then they will hear no more about it-that will be the end of it. But we have not seen the memo, we have not had the meeting and, in fact, we have been stonewalled. The government obviously has something to hide and will not expose the real reason why it gave the contract to the Japanese. It will not explain why hundreds of thousands of manhours, many many hundreds of days of work, have been given to a Japanese firm rather than to a Canadian firm.
The minister mentioned the percentage of Canadian content. The Japanese will not come anywhere near the 50 per cent content while the Canadian firm would have meant 96 per cent. There is a staff of close to 500 in a plant in Belleville which needs this kind of work. It seems to me that the production of three simple memos to explain to some 500 people why work is being taken from them and given to the Japanese is not too much to ask. If the minister and his parliamentary secretary have nothing to hide, then surely these memos should be made available. If they are not made available, then we must assume that the policy of this government is to give work to other countries.

subtopic: INDUSTRY-(A) CANADIAN CONTENT IN MANUFACTURE OF MINING EQUIPMENT (B) CONTRACT AWARDED TO JAPANESE COMPANY
INDUSTRY-(A) CANADIAN CONTENT IN MANUFACTURE OF MINING EQUIPMENT (B) CONTRACT AWARDED TO JAPANESE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the questions I raised with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) were supplementary to the ones asked by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis). They can be found on page 15046 of Hansard for Tuesday, February 16.
The main question I asked was basically why Canadian content of mining equipment for domestic use had fallen from almost 70 per cent in 1970 to a mere 29 per cent in 1980. In fact, if we look at the figures given by the minister two days ago we see that there would be only 27 per cent Canadian content in mining equipment; those are the figures of Statistics Canada for 1980.
There was a $167 million trade deficit in 1980 in mining equipment, and this includes a total importation of some $330 million worth of mining equipment. If we use the minister's figures, $372 million worth of imported mining equipment came into Canada. This is all part of Canada's current balance of trade deficit of $21 billion in manufactured goods, which is having a negative and devasting impact upon the economy and upon employment opportunities for young people in Canada.
There were two basic questions. Why has the Liberal government allowed this deterioration of Canadian content to such a rock-bottom level of only 27 per cent over the past decade? What specific plans does the minister or the government have now to correct this very regrettable situation?
The minister, known as the guru of industrial strategy, has been making promises for nigh on three years in the House now, but he has yet to produce one positive initiative or one shred of evidence that in fact this devastating trend in manufactured products, particularly in the mining sector, is being reversed. Of course we are talking about the kind of
February 18, 1982

equipment which will be in great demand in the next decade as we develop megaprojects in mining, in particular, and in oil sands, coal and various minerals. We are talking about heavy machinery such as the stacker-reclaimers, to which my colleague referred a few moments ago, draglines, bucket wheels, rock drills, ore trucks, compressors, electrolyte cells for processing, crushers, roasters, flotation cells, process control equipment, and various types of conveyers. There is tremendous opportunity here for Canadian enterprise.
We note that our unemployment now exceeds 1.2 million people, that there is an unemployment rate of 17 per cent in the under 25 age group, and that we are experiencing unprecedented lay-offs. These lay-offs have led to massive applications for UIC benefits and claims, thus contributing to the deficit of the Government of Canada.
Since the November 12 budget there have been 2,200 lay-offs in the mining industry, with an anticipated 8,000 by the end of next summer. In British Columbia alone there have been 120,000 lay-offs, 9,000 of them represented by U1 applicants in my own riding, and the number is growing at the rate of 1,600 per month. This $372 million worth of imported mining equipment would produce something in the order of
10,000	jobs per year for Canadian workers. When we look at the tremendous unemployment rate and the deterioration of our economy and compare it with future potential, we must conclude that something is basically wrong. The government opposite is absolutely inept, and there is no obvious answer as to why it wants to export jobs.
What does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce have to offer besides platitudes? Last year he talked about a mining conference in Vancouver with industrial groups. Such a conference took place a year ago and there has been no progress. He talked about beginning a process; I ask, "Where is the action?" 1 hope in response the parliamentary secretary will tell the House what specific examples the Minister of industry, Trade and Commerce can cite of increased opportunity for Canadian manufacturing to provide the very important machinery required in these industries. For example, 1 refer to the stacker-reclaimers, about which we heard, and the car dumpers being used in coal handling terminals on the west coast which are now being increasingly imported from offshore-the car dumpers from Britain, 1 gather, and the stacker-reclaimers from Japanese companies such as Mitsubishi.
Stephens-Adamson in Belleville could produce stacker-reclaimers containing, not 53 per cent Canadian content, but 96 per cent Canadian content and it underbid the Japanese for the Ridley Island stacker-reclaimer by $1 million with a low bid of $19.7 million. That Canadian firm has been denied the opportunity to produce jobs in Canada, specifically in the city of Belleville, Ontario. Instead we are choosing to export those jobs to Japan.
Fednav Com, which is the company set up to operate the terminal, was set up on a non-competitive basis. Its shareholders are well-connected with the Liberal Party in Montreal, 1
Adjournment Debate

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY-(A) CANADIAN CONTENT IN MANUFACTURE OF MINING EQUIPMENT (B) CONTRACT AWARDED TO JAPANESE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon), I am pleased to say that while it is true that Canada has been supplying a smaller share of its domestic market with mining equipment in recent years, this has been compensated to a large extent by growing exports of Canadian-made equipment. Accordingly, consideration of the issue of Canadian content in mining equipment should take into account both the total performance of the Canadian mining equipment industry, including its exports, and the future industrial benefits represented by projected large scale mining developments in Canada.
This trend of increasing exports, offset by rising imports, reflects a process of rationalization and specialization which the industry has been forced to undertake in order to remain competitive in the international environment.
Nevertheless, the rising share of the Canadian mining equipment market being supplied by imports does represent missed opportunities for Canadian equipment suppliers and a significant demand for new mining equipment, which is expected to result from major resource projects, will present many new opportunities for mining machinery companies.
Accordingly, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has undertaken a series of initiatives to assist Canadian manufacturers to seize these new opportunities. In this regard, follow-up initiatives to the Mining Opportunities conference held late last spring in Vancouver have led to more formal linkages between the procurement activities of mining firms and the marketing efforts of suppliers. The department has also established an office of industrial benefits in order to ensure that Canadian firms obtain maximum advantage from large new resource developments. As part of a planned export

market strategy, we have assigned a priority position to mining equipment in several key markets of the world. In this regard, the department has provided assistance under our program for export market development-PEMD-to assist the marketing efforts of 13 companies in some 15 different countries.
Finally, we have also been active in assisting equipment firms to develop new products in order to meet the needs of mining firms in both Canada and abroad. Over $5 million in assistance has been provided to ten firms under the Enterprise Development Program, EDP, to develop a variety of advanced equipment ranging from coal slurry pumps to mine utility vehicles.
It is all right to pinpoint, Mr. Speaker, some of the problems this country has in the field of industrial development or the economy, but it is interesting to find out that action is being taken by this government which will be to the future benefit of the economy.
